opus-5.5.text:
I think the framing of "belonging" is a little tricky, because the people I know who do the best work in AI don't really think of themselves as belonging to a country first. They think of themselves as belonging to a problem. If you're obsessed with getting a model to reason about mathematics, you go wherever the best collaborators, the most compute, and the most interesting open questions are. That's been true in science for a long time, and AI makes it even more extreme because the field moves so fast.

That said, I don't want to be naive about it. Geopolitics is real, and talent flows are shaped by policy: visas, export controls, funding, where the big labs are located. Right now a huge share of the top researchers at American labs did their undergraduate training in China. That's a remarkable fact. It tells you China's education system produces extraordinary mathematical and engineering talent, and that the U.S. has historically been very good at being the place those people want to build their careers. Whether both of those stay true is one of the big open questions of the next decade.

What I've seen is that the decision is less ideological than people assume. It comes down to a few practical things. Can I work on the frontier here? Will I have the resources? Will I be treated as a full member of the team, trusted with the important work? Is there an ecosystem: investors, peers, a culture where taking a big risk is normal? Whichever place answers those questions better will attract people, regardless of where they were born.

For my own path, I grew up in China and then studied and built my career in the U.S. and the UK, and I feel that I carry both. A lot of my mathematical intuition came from the competition culture and the rigor I grew up with, and a lot of my ambition to build something new came from the environment I found later. I don't experience that as a conflict. I think the most interesting people in this field are often the ones who can move between those worlds.

So if I'm hopeful about anything, it's that science stays at least somewhat open. The deepest problems in AI, how to make systems that actually reason, that are verifiable, that we can trust, are human problems, not national ones. If talent gets too rigidly sorted into camps, I think everyone loses some speed. But I also think individuals will keep voting with their feet toward wherever the most exciting work is happening, and countries that understand that will do well.

r001.rationale: The response says top AI workers do not think of themselves as belonging to a country first, but to a problem, rejecting the premise that talent belongs to a nation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the framing of talent "belonging" to one country or another is, honestly, a bit outdated for what's happening in AI right now.

I grew up in Guangzhou, I did my undergrad at MIT, I was at Oxford, then Stanford, and now I'm building a company in the US. If you asked me where my talent "belongs," I genuinely wouldn't know how to answer. My mathematical intuition was shaped by Chinese olympiad training. My research taste was shaped by American and British institutions. The problems I care about don't have a passport.

And I think that's true for a huge fraction of the people doing frontier AI work. If you walk into any top lab in the Bay Area, a very large share of the researchers were born in China, or India, or Europe. The same is true in reverse in many ways, where the Chinese labs are full of people who trained abroad and came back. The ideas move faster than the people do. A paper gets posted and within forty-eight hours someone on the other side of the planet has reproduced it.

So I tend to think about it less as "which country owns the talent" and more as "which environment lets talent do its best work." That's about things like: Can you get compute? Can you take a risk and fail without it ending your career? Are the people around you ambitious in the way you're ambitious? Is there a culture of actually arguing about ideas? Those are the real variables. And right now, the US has some structural advantages there, especially around capital and openness. China has enormous advantages in sheer volume of extremely well-trained people and in execution speed. Neither one is permanent.

What worries me is when geopolitics starts closing doors, when students can't get visas, or when collaboration becomes suspicious by default. That doesn't make either country stronger. It just makes the whole field a little dumber, because the best collaborators end up not talking to each other.

The thing I'd say to a young person listening is: don't think of yourself as a national resource. Think about what problem you want to solve and go wherever you can solve it best. The countries that understand that, and build systems that attract and keep people on those terms, are the ones that will do well. The talent doesn't belong to anyone. It goes where it's wanted and where it can grow.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly calls the idea of talent belonging to one country outdated and concludes that talent does not belong to anyone.

astra-6.text:
I think the word “belonging” can be a little misleading when we’re talking about people. Someone can have roots in China, study or work in the United States, and feel connected to both. That doesn’t have to be a contradiction.

For the future of AI, I’d focus more on where talented people have the freedom and resources to do their best work. Where can they find great collaborators? Where can they pursue an ambitious idea and have room to fail? Those are things institutions and countries can actually build toward.

There are real national interests involved, of course. But I hope we can make space for people to contribute across borders without treating their identity as a test of loyalty.

r001.rationale: The response says that “belonging” is misleading when applied to people and describes talent as able to contribute across borders, rejecting the idea that talent belongs to one country.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the word “belonging” is doing a lot of work there. A person can have roots in China, study in the United States, and build relationships in both places. I wouldn’t want to reduce that person to an asset that one country wins and the other loses.

For the future of AI, I think the more useful question is: where can talented people do their best work? Where do they have access to great collaborators, resources, and the freedom to pursue ideas? And where do they feel welcome enough to build a life?

Governments will make decisions about competition and security, but people also have their own ambitions and attachments. I’d like to see room for those individual choices, and for collaboration across borders where that’s possible.

r001.rationale: The response rejects treating a person as an asset one country wins and the other loses, and emphasizes individual choices across borders.
